uses: Lavender's name is usually traced to the Latin for washing, and its scent has perfumed baths, soaps and toilet waters for centuries. Dried flowers were tucked among stored linen to scent it and to keep moths away. In folk practice the flowers are taken as a calming tea or breathed in to ease stress and invite sleep, and old herbals used them for headaches and an upset stomach. The flowers also turn up in cooking, in vinegars and jellies.
taste: Floral and fragrant; the oil is pungent and bitter
energetics: Culpeper called lavender hot and dry in the third degree
caution_pregnancy: Not enough is known about medicinal use during pregnancy or breastfeeding; avoid. The EMA does not recommend lavender medicines then for lack of data. Amounts normally used in food are likely safe.
caution_medications: Lavender might add to the effect of sedative drugs or herbs. This concern is theoretical, but it matters most before surgery. The EMA reports no known interactions. If you take any medicine, check with a pharmacist or doctor first.
caution_conditions: Avoid it if you are allergic to lavender. Taken by mouth it may cause drowsiness, so don't drive or use machinery if you feel affected. Oral use can also cause diarrhea, headache, nausea or burping, and aromatherapy can bring on a headache or cough. Medicinal use by mouth isn't established for children under 12.
caution_duration: Oral products may be safe short term at the amounts used in studies; long-term safety isn't known. See a practitioner if symptoms continue.
caution_topical: Can cause allergic skin reactions. A few cases of breast swelling in children who used lavender skin products have been reported; it isn't clear that lavender was the cause. Culpeper himself warned that the distilled oil is fierce and should be used only a few drops at a time.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut flower stalks in dry weather when the blooms are open, usually midsummer; morning or evening is best.
garden_water: Dry side; needs sharp drainage and hates wet feet
notes: Likes light, sandy or chalky soil that isn't too rich; heavy clay and overwatering lead to root rot. Cut the plant back each year after flowering. NC State Extension notes lavender is mildly toxic to cats, dogs and horses. Grieve records that lavender was thrown on St John's Day fires to keep evil spirits away.
